prompt:
Here are three short samples of my writing. Match my style in what you write.

Sample 1:
making them play lame chicken.... Now all this done by a young lady who remembers eighteen months ago with so much regret that she has lost so much of her high spirits--might argue that her spirits were before tremendous; and yet they were not. That other Sarah was ladylike, I am sure, in her wildest moments, but there is something hurried and boisterous in this one's tricks that reminds me of some one who is making a merit of being jolly under depressing circumstances. No! that is not a nice Sarah now, to my taste.

The commencement of '61 promised much pleasure for the rest of the year, and though Secession was talked about, I do not believe any one anticipated the war that has been desolating our country ever since, with no prospect of terminating for some time to come. True the garrison was taken, but then several pleasant

Sample 2:
for the best for us in the end; that all has come right in spite of us, we will wonder how we could ever have been foolish enough to await each hour in such breathless anxiety. We will ask ourselves if it was really true that nightly, as we lay down to sleep, we did not dare plan for the morning, feeling that we might be homeless and beggars before the dawn. How unreal it will then seem! We will say it was our wild imagination, perhaps. But how bitterly, horribly true it is now!

Four days ago the Yankees left us, to attack Vicksburg, leaving their flag flying in the Garrison without a man to guard it, and with the understanding that the town would be held responsible for it. It was intended for a trap; and it succeeded. For night before last, it was pulled down and torn

Sample 3:
of the thing. These men our brothers? Not mine! Let us hope for the honor of their nation that Butler is not counted among the gentlemen of the land. And so, if any man should fancy he cared to kiss me, he could do so under the pretext that I had pulled my dress from under his feet! That will justify them! And if we decline their visits, they can insult us under the plea of a prior affront. Oh! Gibbes! George! Jimmy! never did we need your protection as sorely as now. And not to know even whether you are alive! When Charlie joins the army, we will be defenseless, indeed. Come to my bosom, O my discarded carving-knife, laid aside under the impression that these men were gentlemen. We will be close friends once more. And if you must have a sheath, perhaps I may find one
Write an email to a colleague about rumors going around town. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: Re: What they're saying about the mill

Dear Margaret,

I hardly know how to begin, for I have heard so many versions since Tuesday that I am beginning to doubt my own ears. You asked whether there is any truth in the story that the mill is to be sold. I can only tell you what I have gathered, and you must judge for yourself how much of it deserves belief.

Mrs. Hadley had it from her cousin, who is married to a clerk at the bank, that Mr. Pruitt was seen going in at the side door three evenings running, and that he came out looking, in her words, "like a man who had swallowed a stone." Now, what that proves I cannot say. Mr. Pruitt always looks like that. But the rest of the town has seized upon it, and by Thursday it was settled that the mill was sold; by Friday, that it was sold to a Northern firm; and by this morning, if you will credit it, that every one of us is to be turned out by Christmas! How quickly a stone becomes a mountain!

I do not believe it. I will tell you why. Mr. Dawes, who has no reason to flatter me and generally has every reason not to, told me plainly on Wednesday that the books were in better order than they have been these five years. A man does not say so, I think, if he is about to hand over the keys. And yet he did not look at me when he said it. There is the difficulty. Oh, that men should be so provoking!

Still, I will not add my voice to the clamor. It is a poor sort of person who repeats what she cannot prove, and I should be ashamed to find myself among those who are making a merit of being first with the news. Let them talk. Only I would beg of you, my dear Margaret, that if anyone should ask you in the office, you will say that you know nothing, and that I know less. It is the safest answer, and for once, very nearly true.

But I do not like the feeling in the building. The girls whisper at the copier and stop when I pass. Young Thomas has been polishing his résumé at his desk, quite openly, as though he wished to be seen. Is that wise? Is that kind? We shall all be the worse for it if panic is allowed to do what Mr. Pruitt, whatever his intentions, has not yet done.

I mean to speak to Mr. Dawes again on Monday, and this time I shall not let him look out of the window. If I learn anything worth the telling, you shall have it at once. If I learn nothing, you shall have that too, and we will be no worse off than we are now.

Do write soon, and burn this, if you please.

Yours in great suspense,
Sarah
